- When sentiment is consistently negative or near-zero over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 2–5% relative to prior peak.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >5% from prior day), model often overshoots in next 3–5 days; apply downward correction of 3–8% to avoid overreaction.
- If sentiment is positive but recent price action shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), model may overreact to sentiment; dampen forecast by 1–4%.
- Model frequently overestimates in early horizon (1–7 days) when sentiment is volatile; use 3-day moving average of true values to anchor short-term forecasts.
- When sentiment is weak or flat, model tends to ignore downward trends; apply a 1–3% downward bias to forecast if recent 5-day average is below 70.
- For 14+ day forecasts, model often underestimates upward momentum; add 1–3% to forecast if sentiment >0.3 and price has trended up in last 7 days.
- If sentiment is negative and price is rising, model may misread sentiment as neutral; reduce forecast by 1–5% to reflect pessimism.
- Model underestimates volatility in low-sentiment periods; increase forecast variance by 10–20% if sentiment <0.2 for 3+ consecutive days.
